utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner; Julian Nicholls; hiding in the back, Ann Sutherland, just to show that we don't have too many lawyers and as usual, Denise Gustin case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one hiding. Good morning to you. I understand we have Mr. Mayhew this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. He's here and -- but can I just go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. No objection, Mr. Ackerman? Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are in open session. Let me know because I can't check now. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Mr. Mayhew, it's his transcript that will be tendered, and the -- I think we will have to work out the exhibits that were tendered with him -- I'm sorry, through him in the Stakic case. Some of them may have already been tendered in this case through Mr. McLeod, so I'd ask that we -- at the end of his evidence, we can give Your Honour and the Registrar the numbers at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he will be testifying about documents which came to light after he had completed his testimony in the Stakic case. One of which came off his own disc, and it included a document that we already had but with an extra bit added. The caveat had been taken out by ECMM, but he had the original plus some earlier documents. Your Honour, can I say straight away, as you will hear, he only began working for ECMM in March, and some of these documents are earlier documents. Your Honour, what I don't want to have to do is to call yet another witness just to put the documents in. So, Your Honour, unless there is an objection taken by Mr. Ackerman, I'm just going to literally put them in by him attesting that these are the sort of documents that ECMM produced. So there will be some new documents and part of the OSCE report which, although he dealt with extensive parts in testimony, some were left out because they dealt with Manjaca which wasn't relevant to the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem that I see with the proposed way to deal with the documents is the one that I keep referring to, and that is some future lawyer working on this transcript trying to relate the documents we are talking about to an exhibit number. If we don't assign the exhibit number until after the testimony is completed, then everything in the transcript about that exhibit is unrelated to the exhibit number. And that always -- always creates a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will create problems, yes, indeed. But do you think there is a possible solution to that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what -- as I say, I personally will not with one exception be referring to any of the documents that he dealt with in the transcript, because they are there for Your Honours to read. If Mr. Ackerman wants to cross-examine on some of them, then what we'll try to do is assign a number as Mr. Ackerman cross-examines. I can certainly -- I have a note of all the Stakic numbers within the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have actually prepared two of the documents that I know I will use for sure and given them Defence exhibit numbers, and my only concern about that is I didn't want to give them Defence Exhibit numbers if they were also going to be given Prosecution exhibit numbers first, but it looks like that's not going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, except they are. That will create all sorts of -- obviously I was intending that everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather prefer you gave them the usual exhibit number since they were exhibited in Stakic, so that should be easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And any -- I understand there is something else which needs to be given --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They will be -- they have never been exhibited before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Those will be new numbers. And perhaps if Mr. Ackerman knows beforehand what the new number is going to be, that shouldn't pose any problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would then solve the problem. And Ms. Korner's suggestion that there are some documents older than the time he started with ECMM does not bother me at all. I'm convinced they are all authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are waiting I just might say for the record and for Your Honours that I have gone through all of the Novi exhibits and the Novi exhibit book, and I have no authenticity objections with regard to any of those exhibits. And rather than put that in writing, I think I can just announce that that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not the first time you're giving evidence before this Tribunal. You've already given evidence in the Stakic case, so you know what the procedure is. The usher will be handing you the text of a solemn declaration which is -- to us, it's the equivalent of an oath. Please read it out loud, and that will be your undertaking that during the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, please proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. You will be first examined-in-chief by Ms. Korner for the Prosecution, and she will then be followed, I would imagine, by Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin, in this case. Ms. Korner, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, I think your full name is James Barnabas Burke Mayhew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as the Court will see, when we look at some documents, do you normally -- do you normally sign those documents Barney Mayhew, and you're known generally as Barney?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mayhew, you testified in Stakic at length about your background and about a lot of your activities during the period whilst you were working for ECMM, and I'm not proposing to go over that again. But I want to ask you about some further documents that have since come to light from the ECMM archives and I think partly from your own records. I think it's right you only started working for ECMM in March of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I want to you have a look, please, at some documents that were produced before you started work and really just to confirm who the people are and that these are actual reports produced by ECMM. The first report I'd like you to look at is one dated the 1st of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me for just one moment. I'm not sure Your Honours have this. I think we may have to put them up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have a single one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm told Your Honour does have them. You were handed -- or you should have been handed a bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe the Registrar has them because we don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't -- Ms. Gustin tells me that bundles of documents were handed in last week, and it doesn't appear they've got -- this is I think one of the problems about us handing them out in advance; they get lost in the system. Perhaps the simplest way of dealing with there is to put up the documents on the ELMO for the present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I would think so, Ms. Korner that would spare us, but none of us up here do have the bundle that you were referring to, so it hasn't reached us for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I checked with my secretary this morning, she spent almost half an hour --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, but I mean we did hand out the bundle last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mayhew, I think you had a chance to look through these documents yesterday evening after you arrived here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so that the Court understands, this is headed, "Team Doboj." What was Team Doboj?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Team Doboj was a team of ECMM monitors assigned to visit Doboj over possibly one visit or possibly over a period of time, and they were part of the wider group of ECMM monitors based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is not actually going to work, I think, if we have the ELMO -- if you look at the screen --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honours' screen not working either? Can we put it on --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can see on the screen part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll move it up and that way the Judges can see you. It's dated the 1st of February, 1992, which I think is, as you said, before you started work. But if you look, please, at the second page, is there -- there are three signatures there. Do you know these people? Or any of them?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I know Dave Holt, the signature on the left. I know the name. I don't know the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And who was Mr. Holt?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: By the time I arrived in Banja Luka, which was sometime later, Dave Holt was the leader of the Banja Luka group of teams. He was an ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how many teams were there in the Banja Luka -- working in the sort of Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Roughly three from memory. I think it was seven monitors roughly seven, plus the necessary drivers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a daily report dated the 1st of February, which deals with a visit to a town called Donji Vakuf, as is stated, on the way to Banja Luka. Is that a place that you became familiar with at all?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we see that the officials met included the mayor, the president of the SDS, and various other officials and party members who were there. I don't think we need bother so much about the population, which is listed, and there is then a series of problems. And item number 4 says, "There are about 69 refugees in the town, 95 per cent Serbs. They present no problem. They are housed with families and friends." And then if you could look at the second page, please, that states that cooperation between leading parties is generally good, the SDA reported that sometimes the SDS had tried to exercise influence without consultation. And then item number 7, "National conflict is not common." And then finally, the conclusion, "The main humanitarian problem facing this town is the food shortage which seems to be out of proportion with the other towns visited."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be made an exhibit please, which will be 1609? Now, the next document please I'd like you to look at is one dated the 7th of February, so some six days later. Again, a daily report signed by the same people as -- signed twice for some reason, and signed at last. And the subject is a visit to Celinac. The officials met -- the mayor, Kovacevic, SDS; and then R. Brdjanin, SDS deputy chairman then SDP president, SDS; and so on, and the local press. Before we go any further, did you, to your recollection, during your time in Banja Luka or the Banja Luka area ever meet Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can't say whether you did or not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Anyhow, definitely your colleagues did. The general under item 1, "General, though, there had been no problems since the last visit." This was the 2nd. "An increase of refugees from 745 in November, 1991, to 1200 now. No major medical or food or problem with elderly or children." And then, "Refugees are mostly Serbs with some Muslims quartered in private houses." And then it says, "Next visit, CFV investigation." Do you know what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: CFV stands for cease-fire violation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Novska, see new bridge and visit concentration camp to view desecration." Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be made 1610, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, could you look at effectively a weekly summary dated also the 9th of February? And again, just so that the Court understands, were the earlier reports we were looking at, as we can see, a daily report, and then at the end, would there be a summary of all the activities during the week?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I think we can really deal with that very quickly because we see in paragraph 1, the team visited Donji Vakuf, which was that report we looked at. Item number 7, there was a visit to Celinac. And then at the end of the report, if we look at the second page, there was a conclusion that there was 100 per cent improvement on the part of the JNA cooperation. And effectively -- a lot of this report I think is dealing with the cease-fire in relation to the events of Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'd have to look back at page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: When we are talking about cease-fire, generally it referred to the front line running through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be 1611, please. And then the next document, please, 23rd of February, a daily report dated, as I say, the 23rd of February, and it says there was a meeting at Pakrac with -- is that CNG?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that refers to Croatian National Guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the JNA and then it says, "Authorities met at the meeting," and then various places are mentioned, and then we see under Stara Gradiska, General Talic. And again, I don't need to trouble you with the contents so much. Item 5 deals with that meeting with General Talic, but it's mainly, I think, in respect of, again, the Croatian front line, as it were. Again, Mr. Mayhew, did you ever meet General Talic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1612, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the next document, please, the 9th of April. Now, by then, had you actually reached Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely certain as to dates. My recollection is that I arrived in Sarajevo on around about the 6th of April, possibly the 5th, and that I was delayed in Sarajevo for several days because some shooting had occurred there. So it may be that I arrived roughly on the 9th of April or possibly a day later. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we see again Mr. Holt's name on this report and two other people, a Denis Bouttier and a Jerry Krupka. You knew Mr. Holt, what about the other two?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember Denis Bouttier. I don't remember Jerry Krupka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this deals with the current situation in Banja Luka. "Team would leave for Derventa. In Banja Luka last night, at 2400 hours, there were two low order explosions, possibly hand grenades, and automatic small arms fire. This lasted for about half an hour. It was with within 250 metres of the hotel." Was the team staying in the Hotel Bosna, your team?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then there is a report from an interpreter that he heard about a power station having been attacked. And then finally an interview with the UN yielded the information that it is not possible to go from Banja Luka to Belgrade due to hostile blockades. It is understood that this information is from the JNA. When you got to Banja Luka, did you have a problem with barricades?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember there were several barricades of an informal kind, some men on the road, possibly with a make-shift barricade at several points between Sarajevo and Banja Luka, but we were allowed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be 1613, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then next the 18th of April, 1992, this is a situation report. What's the difference between a situation report and a daily report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, a daily report would be put out at the end of each day. In fact, a daily report is a daily situation report or it's a report of your activities that day which would include a report on the situation. The fact that it is titled here, "Situation report" probably means that it is not a daily report but is a report on the situation put out other than at the normal time for a daily report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think this -- you know something about the events here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Item 1 refers to a CapSat and a flak jacket and personal effects of Banja Luka 1 remaining unrecovered. And it goes on to describe that. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recall, Banja Luka 1 was a team of which I was a member. We had been working in Derventa. The situation had become violent. There had been some shelling of the town. We were trying to negotiate with the leaders of all sides to calm it down. An informal front line had grown up between the hotel in Derventa where we were staying, and where we had our CapSat communications machine and as I recall, one of the military leaders. We crossed that front line to negotiate with him. By the time our meeting was over, that front line had become too dangerous for us to return to the hotel, and we were obliged to evacuate back to Banja Luka, leaving the CapSat and these other effects in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then item 2 deals with the JNA and Croatian interpreters. Item 3, "The Banja Luka chief of police told us that police escorts and fuel from the police resources will no longer be provided as of today." Do you remember the name of the Banja Luka chief of police?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I've been reminded by reports that I've read in the -- in preparation for today. I remember Mr. Zupljanin was the name of the chief of police in at least one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then item 4, "The JNA LO," LO being what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "And city officials confirmed that the government of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and Kninska Krajina have decided that EC observers are no longer desired on their territory." This has nothing to -- should that read to do with Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Commander 5th Corps has stated that the -- that EC are welcome to operate in the above areas within five corps boundaries." So are we talking there about the Croatian Krajina as opposed to the Krajina which included Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: May I just take a moment to read it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, I think we are talking about the whole 5th Corps area whose boundaries I don't recall, but I think it's -- and therefore, if that extended into Croatia, then it would refer to Croatia as well as Bosanska Krajina, which is one of the descriptions for that northern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When it was talking about though the government of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, and saying that the EC observers are no longer desired on their territory, can you recall now what was meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, that is the Serb Republic of Krajina and think it should read probably Kninska Krajina from memory rather than -- I think there is an N missing. Is that part of the Krajina which is outside what is now known as Bosnia and within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then Mr. Holt finishes by saying "I have secured a meeting with the mayor for Monday, the 20th of April, at 1000 hours to discuss the fuel, escorts, and whether we can expect to see a similar decision made about banning our services within the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina." And ends, "Have a nice day." Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be 1614.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next can we have the report of the 20th of April, which covers that meeting that was going to be held? It's a daily report. Subject, "Visit to Mayor Radic of Banja Luka. On the 20th of April, at 1000 hours we had a meeting with the mayor of Banja Luka. We updated him on the situation in Livno and then assured him that we, through the cooperation of the EC at Split would continue to deal with the problem of the Serb hostages being held in that area. We asked if the ban of EC activities now adopted in the Serbian Republic of Krajina would be extended to include the Bosanska Krajina, to which he indicated that he valued our work and it was not foreseen." And then, "He was asked to reconsider the question of the provision of fuel by police, and he said but due to shortages he offered that we could have to seek settlement of the claimed theft of some 76 tonnes of fuel, and some tankers owned by the city of Banja Luka by the city of Derventa before he could help. We asked if there would be, and when, elections would occur in the Bosanska Krajina, to which he did not give a direct answer." And then he asked about pursuing the release of a Major Zaric, something to do with Zagreb. And then there was a discussion in respect of Livno, and various permits. Then he talked about refugees, Serbs, and the mayor showed some documents. And then if we go to the next page, please, where we see -- there is a comment, "We feel that since he is receptive to this," this is about working agreements, "And since he is a potentially important figure in the formation of politics to be, it is significant and may be a good basis for future agreements, negotiations on the whole problem." 2, EC activities, "The mayor is satisfied with our activities and is appreciative of our successes. He does not foresee our expulsion from the Bosanska Krajina. He also agrees with the JNA decision of allowing us to operate in the Serbian Republic of Krajina within the 5th Corps boundaries. His staff checked and no new instructions exist from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning this." And then there is fuel, and then the elections. "The mayor did not answer our question directly but went on to explain that a Prime Minister, professor, Dr. Djeric has been appointed along with several ministers." And then the remarks effectively dealing with satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that will be 1615, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the other documents I think you dealt with those that relate to your return to -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I've managed to get my microphone tangled up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Except you were able to produce the complete version of a document in respect of the visit to Manjaca and Trnopolje, and I want to ask you to look at that because a caveat had been removed by ECMM before it was sent off and I think you had the whole document on your disc. So could you be shown now a report dated the 4th of September, headed, "Manjaca and Trnopolje"? I want to deal in fact with the part on Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, although I think this did go in through Mr. McLeod, it was the original version with the caveat removed. So that will have to become another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we deal with Manjaca? Was this a report written by you, as we can see your signature at the end?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Manjaca. The camp at Manjaca, you said, was a military camp, and you described it. "It holds approximately 3.600 male prisoners, about 95 per cent of whom are Muslims. The Bosnian Serb authorities claim that these are prisoners of war. When pressed they defined prisoner of war as those who were arrested in combat zones. Combat zones appear in practice to have been local municipalities with a high proportion of Muslims. As far as we know, there has been little fighting in these areas. Once arrested, according to the camp commandant, the Manjaca prisoners are investigated and if found to be innocent of any crime, they are released to Trnopolje or elsewhere. The stories of the prisoners interviewed without witnesses conflict with the authorities' claims. According to the prisoners, almost all of them are civilians from Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and other nearby areas. They claim that most of them had not possessed weapons. They say they do not know why they are held. Most have no news of their families and believe that their houses are destroyed. "In consequence, all to whom we spoke wished to leave Serb-held Bosnia and rejoin their families anywhere else. The prisoners are housed at closed quarters, in six large cattle sheds. In attitude they are cowed with their eyes deliberately held on the ground until spoken to directly. No visible prisoner bore marks of physical abuse but discipline is evidently extremely strict. Latrines appear to be well constructed. Water and soap are in short supply, leading to prevalent diarrhoea-related sickness. This was named as the top medical problem by the camp doctor who gave urinary tract and respiratory infections as other major problems. Food has, according to the prisoners, dramatically improved within the last week, as the ICRC has been supplying food. The camp commandant said that no provision of any kind had been made for winter, as he hoped the prisoners would all have gone before then. A doctor travelling with the team assessed that prisoners would begin to die rapidly with the onset of winter if they remained in the camp under current conditions." Now, Mr. Mayhew, even ten years on, do you still remember now what Manjaca was like?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see what you said in your report. What impression did it leave with you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It left me the impression that -- that the regime was very firm indeed. I was very struck by the demeanour of the prisoners in Manjaca. I have been into other prisons in different countries, and I have not seen this demeanor elsewhere. For -- I had the impression that for people to be behaving in this way, even when walking along, hands were behind back, very firmly eyes down on the ground, that to achieve that uniformity of behaviour, a very harsh regime would have been necessary. And I was impressed particularly by the fact that this was the day on which a preannounced high level visit was taking place, which -- in which the camp authorities would have wanted to show the camp off at its best.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You recorded that the prisoners were nearly all civilians. From what you saw of them, and obviously -- because you weren't there to see their arrest, you can't say for sure, but did that seem to be accurate that these were civilians as opposed to being fighting men?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think just to be strictly correct, I think I reported that the prisoners said that they were nearly all civilians. Would you just repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. The prisoners told you that they were civilians. From what you saw of them, did that seem to be an accurate description? In other words, that these were not men who had been fighting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It seemed to me credible that that was true for the majority. It seemed to me likely, because of my knowledge of the general situation, that there would be at least some within that camp who had taken up arms, whether or not they were part of any kind of regular or paramilitary force, but my impression again from what they said combined with my knowledge of the general situation. And the way in which they said it made me think that it was highly likely that a very large proportion -- or a large proportion, and I certainly couldn't get into percentages, were civilians who had had no part in any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be made P1616? I'm sorry, can it -- just one -- I should deal with the caveat because that was the reason it was produced. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the end of this report, you added the caveat, "It is emphasised that the team has not yet given the Bosnian Serb authorities an opportunity to tell their side of the story of Kozarac and similar places. Teams hope to do this soon and in addition make a more wide-ranging assessment of the situation in Northern Bosnia. This report should therefore be protected." And just on that note, Mr. Mayhew, first, did you ever get a report from the Bosnian Serb authorities about what they were saying happened in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't think we did, other than the conversations we had with them in the course of this visit and the one that immediately succeeded it, which was in the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May that be made Exhibit 1616?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the final document that I want to ask you to look at again, please, is the report of the mission which you were accompanying with Mr. McLeod, the CSCE mission, to inspect the places of detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was Exhibit 217 -- S217A in Stakic, so this will be 1617/S whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you able to follow, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this report and your knowledge, Mr. Mayhew, caused a little bit of problems in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful to Mr. Ackerman who said he takes no point on what happened at all there. Indeed I was going to point out the way it came out was not in fact the way it was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I think it's right that you saw it at the time it came out and you've reread the whole thing now. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I have reread the whole thing now. At the time it came out, I can't remember whether I read the whole thing or not. I would -- but I think it's very likely that I did, because I was involved in the mission and the mission would have received a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, again I dealt with large parts of this in the Stakic trial. But I think we just need to look, please -- forgive me for just one moment. Yes. The first part was the introduction to the mission and then the background. Yes. Can we go, please, to the seventh page of that report? You dealt with the meeting with Mr. Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, and then you dealt with -- or I'm sorry, you -- the report dealt with, I apologise -- lack of respect for the civilian population. "The mission determined that a complete range of individuals both males and females, young and old, are now being held throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina in various places of detention, and we met with prisoners as young as 17 or even less and as old as 83." And then going on, "There were three categories, prisoners of war. These prisoners have taken an active part in the hostilities and can legally be detained as combatants under the third Geneva Convention of 1949. The mission saw very few of these. It was our impression that much of the fighting was to the death." Obviously this report was based on places that you didn't visit, as you explained, the mission was split. But was that an impression that you got, that fighting was to the death in the area that you visited and you knew, that is around Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I obviously was not present during the fighting except at the edges of it and except by mistake and except when trying to negotiate a deal, a cease-fire between commanders. So I can't comment on the manner and style of fighting. My colleagues and I had the impression at the time that there was not much respect on any side for prisoners, nor for some of the internationally accepted rules of war. Therefore, it would not have surprised us, given our experiences at the time, had prisoners been killed or had there been a refusal to take prisoners and therefore fighting would have been to the death. But that is based on our general knowledge rather than specific observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then there was under B, "people who had allegedly been hiding weapons and/or possessed information of potential military significance." The next page, page 8, please. C, "people who were taken prisoner because they lived or worked in the zone of combat. These people were not taking part in hostilities but were seen as enemies due to their ethnic origin. Their civilians [non-combatant status] should have protected them from detention. This category was easily the largest." Next paragraph deals with stating that, "The mission was not impressed by claims, that they were incarcerated for their own safety or simply because they happened to be resident in a combat zone. Impossible to escape the conclusion that most prisoners are innocent people who have been seized as hostages to promote ethnic cleansing. They are pawns in vicious games played by nationalist politicians." And then the penultimate paragraph talks about, "The destruction of dwellings, local population of one or other ethnic group can never be justified as an action against military targets, a claim that was made to the mission. The ethnically selective torching of houses constitutes in all circumstances a grave violation of international humanitarian law. And military commanders or political authorities who were in a position to prevent such acts should be held legally responsible." Very briefly because I believe you described it to the Stakic trial, I think you, on your visits to Manjaca, Trnopolje, and the other places, saw destruction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: We saw a number of burned-out houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we move on quickly through this, page 9, you dealt with the responsibility of leaders or I'm sorry, I keep saying you. The report, "Despite the existence of warlords, the bulk of the evidence points to the responsibility of acknowledged leaders. The mission believes that in general, leaders exercise effective control over their military and civilian structures. Contrary to what is usually accepted, the so-called uncontrolled elements are marginal. They exist but their importance has been exaggerated by various leaders who find them a convenient explanation for numerous barbarities. The mission had seen camps well organised with military personnel or policemen doing what they were told to do." Is that something that you would agree with from seeing Manjaca and/or Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with this paragraph, which I think is well written on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then as I say if we move through to page 10, "Lack of transparency. Ethnic cleansing operations, which are taking place with official connivance or direct support have left people virtually defenceless even in their homes. Murders, rapes, robberies, assaults and beatings are continuing. Those who carry out these activities are often personally known by their victims and by others in the community. Few have reportedly been brought to justice. Local authorities who profess to be powerless to prevent such abuses and who claim lack of knowledge should not be allowed to continue such charades." Again, did you have yourself, were you present at discussions with such local authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I was present with the CSCE team in all of their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you deal with Trnopolje, but we've already dealt with that in -- it's in the transcript. The treatment of prisoners by authorities and general conditions in the centres at page 11. "With very few exceptions camp authorities have little sympathy for detainees. We witnessed the results of beatings, wounds, fractures, and other injuries in camps controlled by Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian authorities and have reason to believe that innocent prisoners on all sides have been executed. Then the general conditions, "Almost all the centres visited have been improvised and there we see there were stables in Manjaca." You then dealt again with Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: The report deals with Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I keep saying this. The report deals. And then with the conditions there, and then, "Water and food, thus at Manjaca detainees are provided with five only litres of water daily for drinking and bathing." Then the health, if we can look at that at page 12. "In Manjaca, most prisoners exhibit signs of very serious malnourishment, including" -- it's almost as bad as Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think it may be cachexia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Cachexia, hair loss, sunken eyes, and muscle wasting while detainees in other centres are generally less seriously threatened. Detainees in Manjaca admit to weight loss of 10 to 40 kilograms during 2 to 3 months of detention there and in other notorious centres such as the camp at Omarska which the prisoners believe is now closed. In Manjaca and in other locations, the foodstuffs provided have improved during the past two to three weeks due, we believe, to visits by international delegations, the press, and the ICRC." Then I think there is -- the rest -- yes, if we go, please, to medical services at page 13 -- I'm sorry, the bottom of page 12. "It's not too strong to say that the vast majority of the prisoners are living in fear and some in terror of their lives. This is reflected in their behaviour. They react immediately to commands to stand, sit, proceed to the eating places, and in many instances walk like humbled and degraded persons with stooped shoulders and their hands behind their backs. This was particularly evident in Manjaca and Konjic. Previous mistreatment by authorities has undoubtedly broken the spirits of many prisoners. Mental scars are likely to persist for a long time to come." Medical services, and then again, you dealt -- the report dealt with Manjaca. "The hospital ward at Manjaca is completely unacceptable, with the ill and injured accommodated on the floor of a small former stable with only a single blanket for each of their comfort." And then violations, you deal -- or the report deals with violations of international humanitarian law and then recommendations, which we dealt with, plus various annexes. Yes. Thank you very much. And then, Mr. Mayhew, after you dealt -- you accompanied the mission, I think you also - and we dealt within your previous testimony - helped with an air lift of prisoners I think from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: From Manjaca and I think also from Trnopolje and a hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender the transcript, please, as Exhibit P1617? And that report which I've just dealt with is S -- whatever it is /S217. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman will now be cross-examining you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to begin by going through some of the documents that Ms. Korner spoke with you about in the last few moments, and the first one -- basically the same order she went through them, the first one is P1610 -- I'm sorry, P -- okay. It's not the first one actually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, you're right, Mr. Ackerman. It's not the first one. It's the second or the third one. It's the second one actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: P1610. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have it where you can see it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can see the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm interested, sir, in the -- in paragraph 7. First of all, do you know where Novska is?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I refreshed my memory last night using a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good. Tell us. Thank you for doing that by the way.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And this talks about a cease-fire violation that will be investigated in Croatia near Novska, and then adds, "see new bridge and visit concentration camp to view desecration." Now, that part, "visit concentration camp to view desecration" involves a visit, does it not, to the World War II concentration camp of Jasenovac, which had become a museum and which the Croatian forces had desecrated?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember from another report which I read in the bundle that I was reading last night the report of that visit, and it is that report which tells me that it is referring to Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Or Jasenovac. I'm not quite sure how it's pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not referring to any of the camps that are the subject of the 1992 events in the Krajina area, is it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The next document I want you to look at is P1613 -- well, actually let's go to P1612 first, I guess, and then we'll go to P1613. So if we can get them both over there. Now, P1612 is the 23 February 1992 Team Doboj report and Ms. Korner referred very briefly to paragraph 5 of that report. I assume last night when you were reviewing these documents you had an opportunity to read paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the question I have about it is that that paragraph describes, does it not, among other things, a visit with General Talic at what would have been the front lines at that point, and at that point, there was a cease-fire agreement in effect. And this paragraph reveals a rather serious cease-fire violation by the Croatian National Guard, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I need to check a part of the document I can't see at the moment to check if it was during a visit with General Talic. May I see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, you can just pull it off the ELMO or however you want to do it because it's hard to read. It's not a very good copy.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Would you please give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: From a quick rereading here, I'm not sure that it's clear that they were with General Talic when, in paragraph 3, it refers to burnings taking place four to five times nightly. I'm looking at five times nightly which I took to be paragraph 5 there. Do you mean paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. It begins with, "At Stara Gradiska this team met General Talic."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Okay. It is dealing with a reported cease-fire violations in the presence of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And of the monitors?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: And of the monitors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. For instance it says, "It should be noted that the CNG, Croatian National Guard, has advanced far forward of the 3 January cease-fire line at the hill. They were asked to withdraw at the 17 February meeting but at that meeting Lieutenant Colonel Vukovic stated that he did not have authority to comply." And then you go a little further, it indicates, "The team had investigated a reported cease-fire violation and confirmed it because of the fresh dust." And then apparently while they were there, the CNG fired SA, what's SA?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the town showing absolute disregard for the cease-fire and the agreements with the EC about monitors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then, "It's recommended that negotiations be made with a view to withdraw the Croatian National Guard from this" -- it's difficult to read, this -- from something. "They will have to return to 3 January cease-fire line," and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think it says this dominating ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, 1613, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think I have my numbers confused, Your Honour. I think it maybe 1616. I'm looking for the one of 9 April, 1992, and I think that might be 1616 -- no, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is 9 April, 199 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is 1613. I just read it wrong on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. This is the one Ms. Korner was talking to you dated 9 April 1992, and she had asked you if you had arrived in Banja Luka by the date of that report, and you indicated that possibly. It certainly was very close to that date, that you had arrived. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently, there were other ECMM monitors on the scene in Banja Luka before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you actually came there and joined a group that had already been there, including apparently Holt and Bouttier?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you said in Stakic that you were unfamiliar with any activity in Banja Luka by a group calling themselves the SOS. Is that correct? A I don't remember now whether -- I don't remember about that, so I can't be sure whether at the time I was familiar with it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't remember being told anything by the other team members when you arrived there around the 9th of April about recent events involving an organisation called SOS?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now could we look at 1615, please? This document deals with a - among other things - locality known as Livno, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Just looking for the -- can you point out where Livno is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the beginning of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then A talks about shelling and bombing at Livno. Can you tell us where Livno is?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's some considerable distance to the southwest of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And yet when you met with the mayor, he -- I don't know. Were you part of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think not. It is signed by Holt and Bouttier, which implies that I was probably not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When this meeting took place the mayor was expressing some concern apparently about what was going on at Livno. Paragraph 2 basically says that, "The mayor's concern is as follows."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't realise you were asking me a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sometimes I don't put the right emphasis on the end of a sentence to make it sound like a question. Now, Livno, of course, was way outside the borders of the Banja Luka municipality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What the mayor said, that -- about that was that he feared that the Croats wanted to use Serb hostages as exchange for POWs from Kupres and as a shield from shelling and bombing at Livno. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then look at C. "He showed us documentation, we have same -- apparently copies of it were given to the -- stamped and signed by one Mr. Stipe Barun which the mayor claims is being sold at Deutschmarks 2.000 per copy to Serbs in the Livno area. This permits them to leave the area but not to return, in effect confiscating their properties for their lives. These people had the consent of the legal authority, their mayor, Mr. Brkovic to leave but they have been stopped by Mr. Barun the current president of the crisis committee of Livno. The mayor also claims that Barun is an infamous criminal known as the stranger from Split."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Stranger" or "strangler"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Strangler from Split. Do you know anything more about that than we can read there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then finally look at paragraph, it's the second paragraph 2, there are two paragraph 2s. It's the one on the next page, regarding EC activities. "The mayor is satisfied with our activities and is appreciative of our successes. He does not foresee our expulsion from Bosanska Krajina. He also agrees with the JNA decision of allowing us to operate in the Serbian Republic of Krajina within five corps boundaries. His staff checked and no new instructions exist from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning this." So apparently what this indicates is the mayor checked with the higher authorities in Pale and there were no new instructions regarding how your mission should be viewed. Is that the way you read that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, with the only rider that I'm not certain where the higher authorities were, whether they at that stage were in Pale or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Or maybe Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. It's a good time to break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We'll take a break of 25 minutes please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand Your Honours have now got the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and they actually had been delivered, as you had stated, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In open court, Your Honour. I'm not going to start spreading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They got shipwrecked somewhere along the way. We got them with apologies, so that's no problem. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, just before I give you the go ahead, please slow down because the interpreters are having problems. The problem, Mr. Mayhew and Mr. Ackerman, is that you both speak the same language, and the same mistake I'm making myself sometimes when I interject the way I do. So please allow a little bit of an interval between question and answer and vice versa to enable the interpreters to pick up enough time for their interpretation. Because otherwise they have to interpret into B/C/S, Serbo-Croat, and also in French, even though I don't think there is anyone following in French, but that's the position, all right? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, let's both try to do better, even though we might quibble with the proposition whether we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's exactly -- okay. I concede that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want now to spend some -- just a very brief time with the mission report, which is P1617/217. All right. Let's go to page 11. On page 11, the report says, under treatment of prisoners by authorities, "We witnessed the result the of beatings, wounds, fractures, and other injuries in camps controlled by Serbian, Muslim and Croatian authorities." Now, you've -- you told us, and you told the judges in Stakic, that in both Manjaca and Trnopolje, you saw no evidence of beatings of the prisoners. So could I understand that this paragraph, then, refers to other camps that you visited throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think in one of the reports, possibly the transcript that I read last night, and I am not sure which, I said a phrase such as, "Although we saw some people in the medical centre with injuries." And I do recall now also that in the medical centre at Manjaca, there were people with leg wounds, and I don't know the cause of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Other than that, you would agree, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I would agree with what, precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That what I suggested with regard to that paragraph, that it primarily referred to other camps beyond Manjaca and Trnopolje, that you'd been able to visit? Or that someone from the mission had?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that, and the reason for that is that we found out and spoke to different people and saw different people within both Manjaca and Trnopolje. And it's possible that other members of the team present while I was present saw injuries that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please go now to page 13. Now, the fact is that this fall mission to Bosnia-Herzegovina had as its purpose visiting a very large number of detention facilities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think its purpose was to visit as many as possible within the time allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what it was about, to inspect places of detention. And, of course, a great number of them were in fact visited. And there is a list in this document of all the ones that were visited, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had talked this morning about the -- what you believe to be the unique behaviour of the prisoners in Manjaca, the walking with their heads down, their hands behind their backs, stooped shoulders, that sort of thing. The report says there on page 13, you'll see, that this was particularly evident in Manjaca and at Konjic. Were you with the group that went to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that that was a facility where Muslim authorities were holding Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember the details about Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We could actually look back in the back of the document and confirm that. If you look at page 59 -- page 59, it speaks of a visit to Konjic on 3 September of 1992, "Prisoners being held in the sports hall, 167 Serbian prisoners, men of all ages, Konjic, Celebici, 109 Serbian prisoners, and then it speaks of who the authorities in charge of holding them there were, the commander of the Bosnian-Croatian military headquarters, the commanders of the Bosnian-Muslim military headquarters, and then a person named as the director of the Celebici prison." So you'd agree with me that that was a prison in which Serbs were held?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The thing that sort of baffles me is the -- the paragraph describes a characteristic regarding treatment of these prisoners, and let me put it in the exact language of the report. "They react immediately to commands to stand, sit, proceed to the eating places, and in many instances walk like humbled and degraded persons with stooped shoulders and their hands behind their backs." And then it says, "This was particularly evident as Manjaca and Konjic." Now, you know, don't you, that Konjic is near Mostar completely across the country?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember its exact location but I will take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The thing that baffles me, and I don't know if you have an answer, you probably don't but you might, as to how it could be that Muslims in Konjic would house and treat prisoners in almost exactly the same fashion as Serbs in Manjaca would. It's almost like there was an agreement between them as to how to go about this. Do you know if that was some previous existing culture or what?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't know, if I answered that I think I would be speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It is a bit curious, though, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Again, if I answered that, I think I might be straying towards speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I won't make you --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought that was a rhetorical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to talk to you now about various parts of your testimony in the Stakic case, and I think that's something else you've had an opportunity to review before coming in here today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 6.111 you talked about time you spent in Derventa, and you said that when you were there, the town divided itself into an area controlled by a Muslim and Croat coalition, and an area controlled by Bosnian-Serb groupings. Can you tell us when it was that you made that observation, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Would it be possible for me to see a copy of the transcript while answering?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the 18th July, second day, but he'll probably want to refer to both days as we go through this.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Would you guide me to the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Work your way -- it's the second day, 18 July, page 6.111. And don't bother with the fact that it says "not official, not corrected." There has never been an official corrected transcript in the history of this Tribunal. So it's the best we get. Okay? Did you find that page already?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, I have the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just interested in that paragraph that begins at line 3 there. That's what I was talking about. My question is: Do you know about when that was?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: For exact dates I'd need to refer to reports, but having seen the reports last night, it's in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sometime in -- the best I can -- all I'm really looking for is kind of an April 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's in the second half of April, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you get any sense of the state of equipment that the Muslim-Croat coalition had at their disposal? How were they equipped? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any equipment other than small arms, but we did not make an attempt to investigate equipment on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next portion of the transcript I want to discuss with you is just a couple of pages 6.114 starting at line 24 and then going from there. My question is: You did suspect, did you not, that Croatian military authorities were providing arms to Muslims to fight against the Serbs? And what you said on page 6.115 was this: "We were never able to verify arms supplies by anyone, as far as I recall, within the ECMM. We had a strong suspicion that Croatia was supplying arms at least to the Bosnian-Croat forces, regular or irregular, and since the Muslims and Croats were cooperating in Derventa, at least, and elsewhere, as we've already mentioned, we suspected that arms might be reaching the Muslim side as well from Croatia." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You need to also be given the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in March of the year 2000, because I will refer to parts of that also. Keep the transcript there with you, because we'll be going back to it frequently. Your statement on page 2, the third actual paragraph of your statement, near the end, you say that, "During March, I also spent about ten days -- and this would be March, 1992 -- as a member of the team monitoring the cease-fire line in the area of Pakrac and Lipik in Croatia. I was then operating on the Croatian side of the line." Tell the Judges, first of all, just sort of roughly where Pakrac and Lipik are located with reference to the Bosnian Krajina and the area we are primarily talking about.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: They are in Croatia, to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They would be north of, like, Prijedor and that area, just across the Sana River -- the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: If you want me to be precise, I'll need to look at a map, and that will tell us. But it's north of the Banja Luka and Prijedor area in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know how close to the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm not going to guess about a matter of fact, which will be a number of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question that I want to ask you about that: Could you describe the forces that the Croats were able to deploy in that area? What forces did you see? Did you see artillery? Did you see tanks? That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: In the area of Pakrac and Lipik?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember in detail what we saw mostly was infantry units dug in on front lines. I do remember seeing mortars dug in in mortar emplacements at one point. I do not remember whether I saw artillery or tanks. We were, of course, aware of the effects of artillery and witnessed -- examined splash marks from artillery freshly fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So whether you saw it or not, you knew that it was available to those forces?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to the various meetings you had with "Leaders." I think in Banja Luka, and Prijedor, and Derventa, you had meetings with what you described as the leadership of each of the principal groups, that being your words, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. If that's not correct, you can correct me, but my question really is: Could you describe to the courts the purpose of those meetings? Why were you meeting with these leaders?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: We were meeting with them to understand the point of view of the leaderships of all three main sides in the conflict. In order to attempt to report accurately and then to influence the situation towards calming down tension, we needed to have as clear a view as possible of the positions of the leaders, and then to discuss with them ways of calming down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things you have said about these leaders, that's page 3 of your statement, paragraph beginning, "From our visits," you said that the leaders of the three groups often seemed to be drawn from the hard-core element in their respective communities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at no time during any of those meetings did you ever meet with Radoslav Brdjanin, did you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember whether or not I met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the very end of your statement, page 6, what you said there was, "As far as I am aware, I have never met General Talic nor Radoslav Brdjanin."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That is another way of saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Back to your transcript now, and we are at page 6.043, so we are close to the beginning in the first day. At line 12, there is described a meeting that's actually contained in the question. Meeting with Mr. Radic, that would be Predrag Radic; Mr. Zupljanin, Stojan Zupljanin; and the Banja Luka -- who you called the Banja Luka chief of police; and a representative of the army, Colonel Vukelic. Do you recall the meeting with those three persons?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there was a representative there from the civilian authorities, the police, and the military?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that meeting was 23 August, 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: If the report says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what it says. If you want to look at it, you can, but I can tell you that's what it says. Now, didn't you know at that time and all the time that Stojan Zupljanin was not just the chief of police in Banja Luka, that he was a regional -- head of a regional police called the CSB, that covered a fairly wide area, not the same as that of ARK but a fairly wide area of the Krajina, covering police stations in many of the municipalities? You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember at this stage what details I knew about his area of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You certainly knew that Colonel Vukelic came from the 1st Krajina Corps, which had an area of responsibility well beyond the borders of Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I knew that he came from the 5th Krajina Corps, and I imagine that I knew roughly the boundaries of that corps. You must realise that at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this distance, for really hard fact on some of these details, I have to rely on the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: By -- of course by August of 1992, it was no longer the 5th Corps but the 1st Krajina Corps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in a meeting -- in this meeting -- in a meeting of this nature, you were certainly discussing issues that went beyond the boundaries of Banja Luka municipality, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can't now remember whether I did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Going to page 6.169 now. In all these meetings that you had with Serb leaders in Prijedor, Banja Luka, and Derventa, it never became clear to you, did it, that there was, and that they had, an unanimous, single political vision?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's what you said in the Stakic case there on page 6.169. You noticed there were disagreements amongst them as to their aims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember if I noticed that or whether that was our impression from our general experience with the area. Is there a particular line you want me to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, line 5 says, and maybe you meant something different than what I just said. "And there will have been disagreements among the authorities as to their aims."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that. It is a reasonable deduction from our experience of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, I think that if it had been a unified aim of the Serb authorities to massacre the people who were confined in Manjaca and Omarska and Keraterm and Trnopolje n May, June, July of 1992, that there was absolutely nothing to keep them from doing so? They had the guns and the bullets and could have done it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Back now to your statement, we will talk a little bit about Banja Luka. During that period of April and early May, when you were actually in Banja Luka, you never heard, did you, of a Crisis Staff or a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, throughout 1992, no matter where you were, you never heard of an ARK Crisis Staff, did you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I can't now remember if I did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During this time, in April and early May, there was, in Banja Luka, almost no damage of property or other large-scale violence in Banja Luka or its immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was not a city at that time, was it, that could be described as a ghetto for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, I certainly didn't describe it as that. Whether someone else could describe it as that is a matter of opinion.
