utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at DB129, please. Now, Exhibit DB129 is a document that was authored by you and a person named Veldman or Veldman dated 16 September, 1992. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is a document where you and Mr. Veldman were trying to make the case for an ECMM return to Northern Bosnia, apparently an updated version of the effort to make that case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at page 3, under heading, "The delays so far," you say, "In the view of all the monitors who were with drawn from Banja Luka, it was always sufficiently safe for the ECMM to remain in Banja Luka itself." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That implies that you had polled the views of all the people that had been monitors there with regard to their feelings in that regard, and that it was unanimous that they all felt that it would have been sufficiently safe to have remained in Banja Luka throughout the period from May through September when you were authoring this document?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, with the rider that, of course, the monitors had not been in Banja Luka after the evacuation, and so our knowledge was limited, but as far as our knowledge went, that was our unanimous view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You certainly would not have been recommending a state of affairs that would have put the monitors in a very serious physical threat, would you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were actually in Banja Luka, and dealing with various politicians in that area, it appeared to you, did it not, that Predrag Radic was one of the leading politicians in the area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your meetings with him, he spoke frequently, in fact almost invariably, of issues that transcended, went way beyond the Banja Luka municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: For the exact details, please refer to the reports, but we did discuss the position of the entire Bosnian-Serb community within Bosnia and other more wide matters, much more wide-ranging than the Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he provided assistance to you that also went beyond the confines of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was he who provided assistance such as interpreters and police escorts, even when we were operating outside the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said that you were in touch with his office like every two or three days while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had a meeting with him on 13 April, 1992, where he went way beyond the confines of the Banja Luka municipality and went into a very detailed discussion about his concept of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the -- how -- what it would consist of, where the capital would be, very detailed kind of discussion about that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: For the date, I'll refer to the report but I remember the meeting, and we did have a very detailed discussion about future political arrangements within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might -- since we have brought it up, it might be wise to turn this into an exhibit so it would become --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're free to do so, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would become DB130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, what are we talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a document dated 13 April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know, but I'd rather it didn't become a Defence Exhibit, Your Honour, because it's in the Stakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's already in the Stakic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's all going to be given Prosecution numbers. All of this -- all these reports were dealt with in the Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we determine now what its Prosecution number will be, so that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It will be the next one up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What would that number be?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know where we've got to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm very happy with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there will not be a DB130, just for the record. Now, I know there won't be, but just for the record I'm making it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There will be some day but not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You want to go back now to your statement again and we are now up to page 5. And on that page, you're talking about your visit to Manjaca. And during that visit, you of course had occasion to visit with the camp authorities, and one of the things you say about that was, this is in paragraph 3, "They expressed their gratitude to the ICRC for having provided food for the camp." They took it away from you, did they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did they take the transcript away from you yet or do you still have that? Don't let them have that. If they try to take it away, tell them no. It just wastes time. Keep your statement too. You say, "They expressed their gratitude to the ICRC for having provided food for the camp." You see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the time, did you believe that was genuine, that gratitude that they expressed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Second, "They explained that previously they had been unable to provide enough food for prisoners from their own resources." Did you believe that to be a genuine expression?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think I believed that in a difficult situation, authorities in that position have to make choices, when there are not enough resources for all needs. So it was a question of priorities for them rather than absolute inability to find enough food for the prisoners. Sorry, excuse me, I have more to say on this. I believed that food was limited, and I did not know what penalty it would cause to other people who needed food to bring food to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to go to -- back to P1617, and I assume they took that away from you too. And we are going to look at, this time, at page 9 of that document. With regard to the status of the people that you found confined there, what this report says was that "Serb authorities also insisted that they had the right to hold individuals taken in the area of the conflict." Did you hear that expression that they believed they had that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not on the right line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 9, right at the very top, "Serb authorities also insisted."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember the precise wordings used, but I accept this as an accurate record of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall if it was the theory that these people had either been combatants who had disposed of their arms or were trying to become combatants by acquiring arms, and therefore being in the area of the conflict they could be detained?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Would you please restate that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Was the theory behind that, was it your understanding of the theory behind that statement was that these people had either been combatants who had disposed of their arms or were trying to become combatants by acquiring arms at the time they were captured?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: My recollection is that we were simply told that these were people taken in combat zones, and it was not made explicit whether they were doing as you have just described or whether they were simply civilians who were not alleged to have any intention or role in the conflict but who were simply in combat zones. I remember that phrase, "Arrested in combat zones," was the phrase used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in spite of that status that they might have held at that point, they were still permitted visits from the ICRC, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. I think for a fairly short period before our visit, but I cannot remember with certainty whether it is it for two or three weeks that the ICRC had been bringing food or whether it was for two or three weeks only that they had been permitted to visit at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't this claim that they had the right to hold individuals taken in the area of combat, area of the conflict, without further explanation similar to that being put forward by the United States now with regard to prisoners being held at Guantanamo from the Afghan campaign?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Is the Court content for me to comment on United States' justification for its conduct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow this question to be answered. Mr. Ackerman, please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 6.072 of the Stakic transcript now, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated] Transcript, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your visit to Manjaca, you not only observed the prisoners who were there, sir, but you spoke to several of them for, I think you would say, fleeting moments privately, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think for about 30 seconds or so for each person before a guard would approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, Ms. Korner asked you, and she asked a similar question today, the following: "Would you agree that you saw very few people who actually appeared to have taken part in an active part in the fighting?" And you answered, "Yes, that was our impression." My question is: How can you tell by someone's appearance whether or not they have taken an active part in fighting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I didn't say that I can tell by someone's appearance. But I used to be an army officer, I recognise soldiers, and so that gives me some ability to know whether I'm dealing with a soldier, but of course that only goes so far. The principal reason for that being our impression was the manner in which people responded to our questions and the things that they said and the way that that corresponded with my conversations with many civilians over a number of -- over a -- the period of time that I had been active in Northern Bosnia and in the wider region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But Ms. Korner's question had to do with the appearance. The question specifically said, "You saw very few people who actually appeared to have taken part." And you indicated that that was your impression. I'm going to stop there. Isn't it the case that all you really knew about that was that the prisoners themselves told you they had not taken an active part in the fighting? Objectively, that's all you really knew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I would want to pick up this point about appearance. The phrase "appear to" in the way that I use English, perhaps it's our different languages -- can mean physical appearance or it can mean seem to. And it is in that sense that I took the question from Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I was about to rise to my feet and say that is how I speak English as well. "Appears" does not mean appearances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I take back what I said in the beginning, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Oscar Wilde who said we are two great nations separated by a common language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: But to take your question, whether objectively, that is all I really know, it depends on your definition of "objective." That is all I could report as hard fact. However, it's for the Court to decide whether the impression of someone who has relevant experience is objective or can be taken into account as objective or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this about them: Do you think that those people confined in Manjaca knew that if they had not been active combatants, then they could not be held as POWs and perhaps telling you that they had not been fighters would encourage you to help them get released? That's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've said on more than one occasion that one of your problems there was trying to distinguish between truth and lies?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the ways that you might distinguish between whether what somebody tells you is a truth or a lie is to look for what kind of motive they might have to tell you what it was they told you, and if they knew about the rules, then saying to you, "I wasn't a fighter, I shouldn't be here, please get me out," could very well be an untruth but seeking to have them relieved of their current situation. Right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct, but because we had developed some experience, albeit not infallible by any means, in distinguishing when we were being lied to, that was one of the factors we took into account when making up our minds as to what our impression, considering all the factors, was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The people you saw were virtually all of military age, certainly could have been combatants?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they were mostly of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't know if you know the way the system worked in former Yugoslavia, but those of military age would -- large numbers of them at least, would likely have to do compulsory military service with the JNA at some time in their early lives. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I don't remember the details, but I would have known that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so, it's very likely you were looking at people who had in fact had military training, who in fact were soldiers, who had spent time in the JNA and were then parts of territorial units or something like that, kind of as a reserve force?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: At this stage, I can't remember. But I would have taken into account what I knew of these matters at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They certainly could have -- I mean the fact that they didn't have uniforms is totally insignificant. They could have operated as guerrilla fighters, blending in as civilians when necessary and fighting in civilian clothes when the opportunity arose, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And whether or not they were wearing uniforms when they were captured tells you absolutely nothing about whether they were combatants or not. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, because it's -- it's just not going to change anything, Mr. Ackerman. What he thinks about it, what we will decide eventually, and we have to know who we are talking about because it varies from individual to individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, if you look at page 6.076 of the transcript, sir, at line 21, you were even told by Serb authorities in Prijedor that they were facing a group of Muslim extremists fighting a guerrilla campaign against them, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if someone is going -- realises they are going to be captured, a fairly wise thing to do is try to get rid of your weapon and claim that you weren't involved in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the last trial, I got into trouble because I answered questions that were later -- that were then construed as offering an opinion. And I'd just like to check with you whether if I answer that question, it would be construed as opinion and therefore not legitimate, or whether it's a legitimate question for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. Mr. Ackerman, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You even said, didn't you, in your testimony, page 6.075, referring to people that you saw in Manjaca, a proportion of them - you qualified that with a minority - based on what you saw of them, would have felt quite ready to pick up a weapon if available and either defend themselves or take part in offensive operations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Would you please refer me to the line?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's 6.075.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think you need to go back to make sense of this to look at 6.074, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It begins on line 25 on 6.074 and continues over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you need to look at it in the context of the question asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's correct that you said what I quoted there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. While you were at Manjaca -- actually that's not the true question. Let me -- because this wasn't while you were at Manjaca. You were at Manjaca when?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: In late August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then it was when you were there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Or may have spilled over into early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While you were there, you learned that a nutritionist had been provided to the camp and would remain there for at least ten days, maybe more, to improve and monitor the quality of the meals being provided, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember all of that except for the ten days. I don't know the exact time period but I know that it was for some time going forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to refer now to some parts of Exhibit P1616. First of all, the first part of that report, this is a report that you authored yourself. The first part of that report deals with Manjaca, and in the second paragraph, regarding Manjaca, the last sentence, you speak about having spoken with various of these prisoners, you say this: "In consequence all to whom we spoke wished to leave Serb-held Bosnia and rejoin their families anywhere else." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you go to page 2 and it deals with Trnopolje. And you say that the centre is run by the local Red Cross and has no visible internal discipline. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 6.159 in your testimony in Stakic, you are talking about your visit to Trnopolje and in line 12 you say this: "We noticed that the barbed wire fence had been recently removed from Trnopolje." Now, I know there is an explanation for that but the thing that came to my mind when I saw that was how can you tell by looking at a place that there had been a barbed wire fence there that had recently been removed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I recall fence posts still being in place, and you can tell if a wire has recently been cut. I do not remember the exacts detail, but I think that it was a case of fence posts with pieces of wire still on them, but the main part of the wire removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if the wire was still on them, you would have been able to tell whether it was barbed wire or not, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: If there was enough of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did you -- where did you get this idea in that answer you gave in Stakic that the wire was barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: On reflection, I think I got it from the CSCE mission report, which I think I'm right in saying mentions barbed wire. And the other reason would be that it would be unusual for a prison camp not to have barbed wire because it will not prevent escape. I'm not aware of a prison in similar circumstances without barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you still have the mission report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's being brought to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at page 47. Under the heading, "Facility," I think you'll agree with me it does not say "barbed wire," it just says "fencing"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct. It may be that my memory of this report is faulty, but I think I remember that in some part of it, it refers to barbed wire. But as I made clear in my earlier reply, it's what I think I remember. It's not an absolute claim to certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any impression that the entire Trnopolje complex was at one point surrounded by barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: My impression at the time was that it had been completely surrounded by barbed wire and that that had recently been removed. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you leave room in your mind for the possibility that you're incorrect about that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: By using the word "impression at the time," I leave room for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've heard earlier in this case about how the people in Trnopolje had to live outside night and day. It's your view, is it not, that it was to their advantage to live outside and would continue to be until the weather became cold in the winter?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Did I say that in a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 6.092, Stakic transcript. Also in a statement.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I recall something about this, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think if you look at 6.092, line -- starting with line 2, what's actually being done there is a quote from something that you yourself had written.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think it is a quote from the CSCE mission report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You could be right about that. In any event, do you agree with that proposition? Rather than trying to find out where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: In general, it is better if people are housed in buildings. We all know that. I think what the mission report was trying to say is that under the circumstances, being in the open air had some benefits as well as some obvious disadvantages, in terms of protection against the weather. And I again -- remembering my previous experience, I think it is probably not for me to say what they thought the benefits were, but fresh air speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you still have the report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 10, Ms. Korner read the first half of the paragraph beginning with, "Local authorities." It goes on to say this: "At the same time, we cannot allow them to close their camps and push the unfortunate inmates into the danger-ridden regions where social predators remain at large." You remember reading that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was a real situation, wasn't it, and a real concern?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: You mean a specific part of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That, what I just said about ECMM had a concern about if the camps were closed and the inmates were just put out, outside the gate, that they would be prey to what they call the social predators who remain at large?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It was the CSCE mission that had that concern but yes, it was their real concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. 6.024 of Stakic is where we go now. That part in your testimony in Stakic, you were speaking of your mission, as you arrived in Bosnia. You said you first were trying to understand a complex and changing situation. And one of the things that you decided would be beneficial was to try to verify rumours that would circulate regarding atrocities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was because these stories of atrocities, these rumours of atrocities, would get people stirred up, get people angry, and cause them to want to seek revenge?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you hoped that by, as quickly as possible, discovering the truth regarding these rumours, that in some instances, at least, by making the actual truth known, that you could calm the situation and avoid the inevitable consequence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you described this business of false rumours as a very major and important feature of the situation as you found it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You gave an example of a rumour, just a hypothetical, a rumour comes into a village that two Serbs have been killed by Croats. You say, "The Serb community would get furious and frightened, the rumour would go around, and quite often they would then organise some sort of retaliation in their town against the Croat community." When you say "they would then organise," and that's 6.025, line 6, some sort of retaliation, when you say, "They would then organise," that could simply be anything from the authorities of the town to a group of concerned citizens, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes, or other groupings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. As you said, in Stakic, it's perfectly possible that there were a number of isolated incidents of atrocities which realistically the authorities could do little or nothing about? You'll find that at 6.081, if you want to check it.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember that and I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you'll agree that in many cases of these kinds of incidents, it could be extraordinarily difficult, if not impossible, to ever even identify the persons involved in that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I've no objection to answering that question, but again my -- I wonder if that's in danger of me straying into expressing an opinion or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In this case, I would invite you to answer the question, because it's partly, if not mainly based on your personal knowledge of the circumstances and the environment at the time. So what you're being asked to give us information about is quite legitimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And revenge -- in these instances, as hard as you all were trying, revenge could actually have been taken before the situation, before you would ever have a chance to come, try to calm the situation by ferreting out the truth?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And many of the rumours that were circulating around were just never checked out by you or anyone else to your knowledge, were they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly more of a job than your small team could handle, but you were doing the best you could? That's fair, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's quite fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And I think what one can sort of glean from what you've been saying about this, and what you said about it in your prior testimony, that one of the problems was that people, uncritically, with virtually no scepticism would believe these rumours, and you basically said that on page 6.079, where you said in line 20, "Virtually all stories about atrocities are believed."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There seem to be an inability or an unwillingness to question. There was just this immediate tendency to believe the story?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: In general, that was our clear impression and experience, although of course there will be a variety of reactions. And I'm sure there were some people who were not so quick to believe every rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we've talked about how many of these were never able to be followed up or checked out to determine whether or not they were true, and I take it you'd agree that it's likely that some of those rumours which probably weren't true persist even today in the minds of the people who live there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I agree that that is likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told the Stakic court that most often when you were able to check these rumours, quite often something had been done but on a much smaller scale, that you would report back, and when you reported back the truth, that that frequently had a calming effect on the situation, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Would you please refer me to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope I can. It's probably 6.079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Anyway, let's not waste time on this, Mr. Ackerman. Just put the question as direct as you would like to, without referring to what he had stated to the Stakic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the position would, I assume, remain the same for him, and he would be able to give us an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you can give an answer without me asking a further question, can't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's just that word "frequently" that made me look for the line. We did sometimes have a calming effect, but of course we were very conscious that it wasn't anything like frequently enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it's while you were doing what you were doing that you could have this calming effect and avoid a retaliation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: The answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 6.026, you, in the Stakic court told about a situation that occurred in Derventa, a place where the front lines basically went through the middle of the town. You had spoken to a Serb military commander who told you he had reliable information that 400 Serbs were being held in a basement in Derventa and forced to give blood for wounded Muslim forces, and that he was ready to use all means at his disposal to launch an attack to stop this atrocity. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you said that you went to that basement, you checked it out, that you found eight Serb prisoners, none of them giving blood, you reported this back to the commander. He accepted your word about that and did not launch the threatened attack.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. It was my colleagues who did the verifying, but I was involved in the discussion with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You've been asked about this previously. It's in the CSCE mission report, page 4. It's in the background part of that report, where it's written, "This is not an impersonal war. It is a civil war between communities for territorial expansion and ethnic supremacy. The first casualty has been good neighborliness and compassion, the second, truth." And you've indicated previously that you agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I think it's well put.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And truth was a casualty because, as the report later says on page 5, facts and truth have become enmeshed in partisan distortion, and says, "This is possibly an unduly gentle way of expressing the reality." You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Lord Owen spoke in the introduction to his book and you've probably read it, he said, "Never before in over 30 years in public life," speaking of his experiences in Bosnia, "Never before in over 30 years in public life have I had to operate in such a climate of dishonour, propaganda, and dissembling. Many of the people with whom I have had to deal in the former Yugoslavia were literally strangers to the truth." That pretty much matches your experience, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It matches much of my experience there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your precise and concise answers. That's a rare event in this Court, and we have finished in good time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner, do you have re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour, and it goes back to the document DB129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, I don't know if you've still got that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Nor do I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's your report of the 16th of September. As has already been pointed out, you were writing that with a view to persuading ECMM to return to Northern Bosnia. Had you spoken to a number of people before writing this report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Very likely. I was in the headquarters of the ECMM and speaking to some of my colleagues every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at what you said about the minorities view from Banja Luka? It's paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Can I read it here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it needs to go on the ELMO. "Both the Catholic bishop and the Muslim mufti said that for their people the situation had worsened sharply after ECMM's departure at the end of April." Is that the Catholic bishop and the Muslim mufti in Banja Luka that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "They were extremely keen to see us return permanently. Large tracts of land not far from Banja Luka and also further afield have been dramatically ethnically cleansed since April." Was that what they -- was that what they said to you or what you were able to observe yourself from what you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: It's not exactly 100 per cent clear from this text, that's no doubt why you're asking the question. I cannot now remember whether the bishop and the mufti told us that. So it is possible that either they told us that or -- which would not be surprising, or we had that from the many other sources that were reporting similar things at the time, or both.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The process reportedly still continues with considerable momentum. Religious leaders meet the authorities regularly but elected minority political leaders say they may not. Again, Mr. Mayhew, it may not be the clearest sentence, with the greatest of respect. What was actually being said there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, religious leaders meet the authorities regularly, that's clear, but elected minority political leaders say -- and I don't remember whether this was directly to us, or were reported to have said, reported perhaps by those religious leaders, that they are not allowed -- they were at that stage not able to, not permitted to, meet the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. All right. Yes. And I think that's -- well, perhaps you could just read the last paragraph, please, paragraph 16. "The need for urgency. It is a straightforward if emotive fact that every day more people are killed on the front lines, more are evicted from their homes, more homes are destroyed, and winter moves closer. No other organisation is currently as well placed as the ECMM to report on and tackle these problems at their roots." Did you -- did in fact ECMM return to Northern Bosnia after this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Not in any -- not with any permanently deployed mission for the remainder of my time, which was up until I think March of 1993. We may have had some few day missions or very short little missions in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayhew, that's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. There are no questions from the bench, and that means that your testimony comes to an end here. I should like to take this opportunity to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal for having come again this time in a different case to give evidence. And I need barely tell you that you will receive all the assistance that you require to enable you to return wherever would you like to go to. Thank you, and the usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Korner, just the confusion is mine not anybody else's. Next witness is 7.110. 7.210?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next one is 7.210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just out of precaution, I brought both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This one I think we had agreed we will hear her first in closed session to determine whether it's a case of continuing or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls will be calling her, Your Honour. I don't know whether Your Honour wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will take a break now and when we are about to return, Madam Chuqing, please, just prepare the courtroom straight away so that we will waste as little time as possible. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into closed session for a while. Until we decide whether we will continue with closed session or not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I just remind the counsel to switch off the microphone when the witness is answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The document can come off the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in open session now. Mr. Nicholls, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you some questions about an event that took place in Omarska after you'd been there for some time. At one point, was there a delegation which arrived at -- excuse me, at Omarska camp, that sticks out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can the interpreter go to channel 7? Because we are having voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are ready, yes. We are on channel 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I can be heard now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I can hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again. Do you remember a delegation arriving in Omarska camp after you'd been there for some time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember that delegation very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On channel 8, I am not hearing any distorted. I don't know how it works but I'm hearing the witness's voice first, then somebody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't expect you to remember the exact date but approximately when did this delegation arrive? What month and if you can tell me, what part of the month?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: I remember it well. It was in the month of July, around the 15th of July, a day before or a day after the 15th. I remember a high-ranking delegation arrived at Omarska, and everything at the camp was arranged to meet the delegation. As far as I can remember, they arrived around noon. I could clearly see the camp commander, Zeljko Meakic, wearing his parade uniform, blue with cap with a fringe, saluting to the high-ranking delegation. And since for the entire duration of that time, I was at the canteen, together with other women, and the restaurant had glass walls, I could clearly see all the members of that delegation. They were Radoslav Brdjanin, Vojo Kupresanin, Radisav Vukic, Stojan Zupljanin, and Momir Talic. On the tarmac outside the canteen, a choir was lined up, made up of inmates, living skeletons, who, while the delegation was passing, sang Chetnik songs such as, "Who is talking, who is lying, that Serbia is small?" And held three raised fingers crying, "Long live Serbia, long live Yugoslavia." And sang other Chetnik songs as well. The song reverberated through the camp. We, the women, were sitting in the canteen and observing all this. The delegation then went upstairs where the personnel of the camp were sitting down. How long they stayed upstairs, I really cannot say now, but they remained there long enough for me to be able to see clearly the persons I have enumerated. In that choir, I saw a lot of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a second and go back over some of the material you've just talked about. How -- if you can describe -- and I'll show you a diagram in a moment to help you, but how did this delegation arrive? Were they on foot? What kind of vehicles did they arrive in?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Near the canteen, I saw them coming, escorted by a special unit which was normally not stationed at the camp. There was talk about some sort of special intervention platoon, which came specially for that delegation. They were wearing blue uniforms, to the best of my recollection. I could clearly see an APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could show the witness, P1128.4, which is a diagram, if that could be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Witness, if it's easier, you can look at the exhibit to your right, just on the ELMO. That's a photo of a model. If you look at that for a second, can you tell me whether that's a fair and accurate portrayal of Omarska camp as it was in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes. I can see the canteen here, the rooms upstairs where interrogations of prisoners were conducted, the room where we slept. I can see the "white house." I can see the tarmac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to just make a mark, make an X, on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is the document, the exhibit that she has, already a marked exhibit? Do you have a spare copy that you could give her and she would put the markings on that spare copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you prefer, she doesn't need to mark it. I just want it to be very clear to you what her position was. It doesn't necessarily have to be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if I missed it but would could you just please mark -- just point to where you were when this delegation arrived.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: [Indicates] [Microphone not activated] This is where this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters may have missed the beginning because the lady was turned away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, please, could I ask you to start again? Start your answer, your reply, from the very beginning, because the interpreters missed the initial part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is the canteen where I was spending time with other women. At the moment when the delegation arrived, I was here, right here. Zeljko Meakic, camp commander was standing here. And this is where he was standing as he was saluting the delegation. And I was here for a while before I walked to the other side of the canteen to observe the choir which was standing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think [Microphone not activated] An indication of what she has shown us would be difficult. I think you ought to give her a fresh copy and we ask her to mark on the copy that you will give her, Mr. Nicholls, because otherwise we will get a confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have another one available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Usher, please remove the previous one from there. Hand it back to the Registrar. And, Witness, I'm going to ask you again, this time, take a pen, show us with -- and put a number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, if you go here again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put a number 1 against -- okay. That's where you were? Together with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please mark on that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several of us standing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please mark with a number 2 where Meakic, according to you, was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I take it that you moved to the backside of the canteen, or could you explain your movement in better language? And perhaps draw the position by means of an arrow and a number 3? Did you move alone or together with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I walked to the backside alone but there were other women here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And where would that be? Where did you go to? Could you mark it with a number 3, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this side to the opposite side, where there was a table and two chairs, where we women who weren't working that day in the canteen used to sit. It's not very convenient for marking on this particular photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I asked to you put an arrow, and then behind the arrow, you put an arrow pointing to where you were, and then behind the arrow put a number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but the arrow must be on the light blue part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another photo which may help to understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't understand the difficulty that she is encountering. Now, with your pen, can you point at where you went to? Don't write anything for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop where you went to, the place where you went on your own. There. Okay. Now can you just draw out of that spot into the blue area, a line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, and mark number 3 at the beginning of that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. More or less we have handled it. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were at position 1. At number 2 is where you saw the greeting. I'm going to ask you: For how long were you observing this delegation when you were at position 1 looking out the window?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly how long it lasted, this salute and greeting of the delegation before they moved on towards the tarmac in order to hear the choir singing. I really can't give you an exact time but it was long enough for me to see what it all looked like. It was ten, maybe 15 minutes. I can't be more exact than this now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when the delegation moved to where you say this was this choir, and I'll ask you to describe that in a minute, were you able to watch them walk from the point you've written as 2 to the other side of the -- around the corner of the building?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Correct. I was perfectly able to see it, and I saw them coming, and then they turned to face the choir. I had a feeling that they were talking to the inmates in the choir, but the singing was too loud for me to hear the discussion between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this entire time, you were inside this building you call the canteen, the restaurant, and you walked inside there just to look out another window as the delegation moved?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW
utterances.text: Yes. The canteen was glazed. It had glass windows and walls on all sides. I was inside all the time, and no matter where you are located at the front or at the back, you can see clearly what's going on outdoors at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nicholls, we need to stop there because we have already overstepped. Witness, we will continue tomorrow morning. Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, I told you last week that I was trying to have the sittings of the 3rd -- of the week starting the 3rd of February, to shift it to the morning. That's what's going to happen. We will have five morning sittings. If you have difficulties in your case and you would like any one of those to be sent back to the afternoon, because of what you explained to us as being your difficulty, Mr. Ackerman, then let us know and we'll shift one or more of them to the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it would require that at all. It might require that we adjust the breaks a little bit so that I can take care of some business I have to do at 11.30. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before Your Honour arises, could we have a ruling fairly shortly because of witness organisation, as to whether Your Honour is going to grant Mr. Ackerman's request for the break in February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't discussed it with the other two judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking. Your Honour, we need a fairly quick decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We haven't discussed it as yet. I hope to discuss it between today and tomorrow, and we should be able to come back with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just before we break could we have this exhibit, which has now been marked, remarked as 1128.4/1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's 1128, okay. Perfect. We are going to leave the courtroom. Madam Chuqing, the necessary precautions before the witness goes out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
